nameStory: "Hoary" refers to the silvery-white, fuzzy coating on this plant's leaves that makes it look frosted or aged, like gray hair on an elderly person. The name "mugwort" comes from the old practice of using related Artemisia plants to flavor mugs of ale before hops became popular. It's also called "Dusty Miller" by gardeners who love its silvery appearance in flower beds.
description: Hoary mugwort is a low-growing perennial herb with distinctive silvery-white, deeply lobed leaves that look almost ghostly against darker vegetation. Originally from Asia, this coastal wanderer has made itself at home along New England's sandy shores and dunes. The plant typically grows 1-2 feet tall and spreads to form silvery patches that catch your eye from a distance. In summer, it produces small, inconspicuous yellowish flower heads, but most people notice it for its striking foliage rather than its blooms.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided, almost lacy leaves covered in dense white or silvery hairs that feel soft and woolly to the touch, like velvet or felt fabric

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats or clumps that hug the ground, rarely exceeding 2 feet in height

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny yellowish flower heads clustered in branched spikes, easily overlooked and much less showy than the silvery foliage

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Entire plant has a soft, fuzzy texture due to dense white hairs; leaves feel thick and substantial, not papery

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Unmistakable silvery-white to gray appearance that stands out dramatically against green surroundings

habitat: Look for hoary mugwort along New England's coastline, especially on sandy beaches, dunes, and coastal bluffs where salt spray and shifting sands challenge most other plants. It thrives in well-drained, sandy soils and full sun exposure typical of maritime environments. You'll also find it in coastal grasslands and sometimes in inland sandy areas, particularly where it has escaped from cultivation in gardens.

seasonality.spring: New silvery foliage emerges, looking fresh and bright white as the growing season begins.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size with maximum silvery effect, and small yellowish flowers appear in July through August.
seasonality.fall: Foliage may become less silvery and more grayish as the season progresses, but remains distinctive.
seasonality.winter: In milder coastal areas, some silvery foliage may persist, making it identifiable even in the dormant season.

funFact: This plant is nature's own living air freshener - crush the silvery leaves and you'll smell a pleasant, sage-like aroma that was once used to repel moths and fleas, earning some Artemisia species the nickname "fleabane."
confusionNotes: The silvery, woolly foliage might remind you of lamb's ear, but hoary mugwort's leaves are much more deeply divided and lacy rather than simple ovals. Remember: hoary mugwort has "fancy fingers" (deeply lobed leaves) while lamb's ear has "simple mittens" (undivided oval leaves).
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this with the "Dusty Miller" commonly sold at garden centers (Senecio cineraria), which has similar silvery foliage but different leaf shapes. Both share the common name because of their dusty, silvery appearance, but they're different species entirely.
compareHints: Unlike common mugwort which has green leaves with white undersides, hoary mugwort is silvery-white all over and much more compact. Field sagewort also has silvery foliage but grows much taller and has very narrow, thread-like leaf segments rather than hoary mugwort's broader, lobed leaves. Sweet annie is completely green with feathery, aromatic foliage and lacks any silvery coloring.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's Artemisia species, common mugwort is the tallest and most common, with the most deeply divided leaves.
Among New England's Artemisia species, field sagewort stands out for its preference for the driest, sandiest soils and its exceptionally finely-divided silvery leaves.

Silver wormwood stands out from its New England Artemisia relatives by its intensely silvery-white appearance - common mugwort has green tops to its leaves, while hoary mugwort is more coastal and has different leaf shapes.
Among New England's wormwoods, Sweet Annie is unique for its sweet fragrance and annual growth habit - most other wormwoods are perennial and smell bitter.
Absinthe wormwood is much more silvery and aromatic than common mugwort, which has green leaves with white undersides.
Among New England's Artemisia species, biennial wormwood has the most finely divided leaves - much more delicate-looking than the broader-lobed common mugwort or the silvery hoary mugwort.
